answer_text:
Let “inside the unit circle” mean \(|x|<1\). We count solutions in the open unit disk.

Make the substitution

\[
z=x^2.
\]

Then \(|x|<1\) iff \(|z|<1\), and the equation becomes

\[
z=e^{-z}.
\]

Thus we need to count fixed points of

\[
T(z)=e^{-z}
\]

inside the unit disk \(D=\{z:|z|<1\}\). Once such a fixed point \(z_0\) is known, \(x^2=z_0\) will give two solutions for \(x\), provided \(z_0\neq 0\).

Suppose \(z\in D\) is a fixed point of \(T\), so

\[
z=e^{-z}.
\]

Write \(z=r+is\). Taking moduli gives

\[
|z|=|e^{-z}|=e^{-r}.
\]

Since \(|z|<1\), we get \(e^{-r}<1\), hence

\[
r>0.
\]

Also, \(|z|<1\) implies \(|s|<1\). Now compare imaginary parts in

\[
r+is=e^{-r-is}=e^{-r}(\cos s-i\sin s).
\]

We obtain

\[
s=-e^{-r}\sin s.
\]

But for \(|s|<1\), \(\sin s\) has the same sign as \(s\). Therefore, if \(s>0\), the right-hand side is negative; if \(s<0\), the right-hand side is positive. The only possibility is

\[
s=0.
\]

So every fixed point of \(T\) in \(D\) is a positive real number \(r\in(0,1)\) satisfying

\[
r=e^{-r}.
\]

Now use fixed point theory on the real interval. Any such \(r\) lies in

\[
I=[e^{-1},1].
\]

On this interval,

\[
T(r)=e^{-r}
\]

maps \(I\) into itself, and

\[
|T'(r)|=e^{-r}\le e^{-e^{-1}}<1.
\]

Hence \(T\) is a contraction on the complete metric space \(I\). By the Banach fixed point theorem, \(T\) has exactly one fixed point \(r_0\in I\). Therefore \(T\) has exactly one fixed point in the unit disk.

Thus the equation \(z=e^{-z}\) has exactly one solution \(z_0=r_0\) with \(|z_0|<1\). Since \(r_0>0\), the equation

\[
x^2=r_0
\]

has exactly two square roots,

\[
x=\pm \sqrt{r_0}.
\]

Moreover, \(r_0<1\), so

\[
|x|=\sqrt{r_0}<1.
\]

Both lie inside the unit circle.

Therefore the number of solutions is

\[
\boxed{2}
\]
